request.title: BoRHeZ Studio Original #003 — Creative Council blind competition
request.prompt:
Create ONE fully playable original HTML5 mobile minigame through the NEW three-proposal/critic/Producer concept-selection pipeline. This is a live integration test of the upgraded autonomous studio. Let Designer, Researcher and Engineer independently invent distinctly different game ideas; have Critic assess each and Producer commit to one selected proposal before coding. Preserve the winning and rejected proposals with explicit reasons in the release receipt and dashboard.

All artistic and gameplay choices, including actual public game title, genre, art, rules, score and replay structure, belong to the agents. Choose a SIMPLE, intuitive, FUN, lightweight portrait-mobile game playable with one finger. Prefer a genuinely fresh interaction over a cosmetic reskin. Avoid Cataclysm's survival combat, Neon Salvage's collect/dodge, Peach Bounce's paddle and tile breaking, and Threadlight's ordered needle/path embroidery. The new game should still feel fundamentally different from all four.

A real working game is required—not concept art, a technical demo, a proposal or empty UI. Use only HTML/CSS/JS in the permitted directory docs/games/studio-original-003 with no external assets, authentication, network services, ads, analytics or paid runtime calls. Match existing factory constraints: responsive at 360x780 and 390x844, usable touch pointer cancel/re-entry, visible score and state, start, pause/resume, restart, a clear goal and a short end condition, with reduced-motion support. Keep technical logs/agent reasoning records outside the game surface.

Independent browser acceptance and QA must verify not only standard controls but that the IMPLEMENTED game actually matches the Producer's selected pre-coding concept. Publish only tested accepted source with a dedicated stable URL and linked creative decision on the dashboard. If creative-decision validation fails, stop and expose diagnostics rather than quietly substituting a concept.
acceptance: Three independent concrete concepts from Designer, Researcher and Engineer are recorded before critique and coding; each includes a real named mechanic and scoring/end rules.
Critic compares all three concepts with strengths, risks and mitigations; Producer selects exactly one, explains both rejections and issues binding implementation directives.
Coding agent implements the named Producer-selected game and documents concrete features that realize its core loop; independent QA rejects an unrelated game.
The resulting complete minigame is original, differs fundamentally from all current BoRHeZ titles, and can be understood and controlled with one finger.
Both 360x780 and 390x844 Chromium mobile-emulated touch acceptance runs pass with no resource/JavaScript errors or visible interface overflow.
Start, pause/resume, restart, score, actual gameplay response, correct state reset, real end condition and stable diagnostics function.
No runtime third-party assets, network dependencies, logins, telemetry or payments; game remains self-contained within permitted HTML/CSS/JS files.
The accepted game is listed on the dashboard with a stable play link and an inspectable creative decision, and exact live bytes are verified before reporting delivery.

designer.claim: Proposing a unique, tactile, one-finger mobile game where players 'capture' and 'weave' light threads into patterns by dragging a glowing orb, differing fundamentally from existing BoRHeZ games.
designer.rationale: This concept centers on a continuous, smooth dragging interaction that requires precision and rhythm, offering surprising tactile nuance as the glowing orb attracts and ‘weaves’ light threads dynamically based on player motion. The visual theme involves luminous, abstract threads on a dark canvas, creating a mesmerizing aesthetic different from combat, dodge, paddle, or ordering mechanics in prior BoRHeZ games. The clear scoring system incentivizes pattern completion within a time limit, giving a short but rewarding round-based game cycle suitable for mobile one-finger play.
designer.objections: Potential issues include ensuring the dragging mechanic remains intuitive and responsive on small mobile screens, avoiding player fatigue from requiring careful precision, and balancing difficulty so it’s engaging yet accessible. Another concern is that the visual complexity might impact performance on low-end devices if not carefully optimized.

concept.title: Lumen Weave
concept.core_loop: Player drags a glowing orb along the screen to attract and connect scattered light threads forming dynamic luminous patterns. Completing full patterns scores points and triggers new random thread arrangements. Each round lasts 60 seconds, challenging players to weave as many patterns as possible.
concept.player_action: Use one finger to drag the glowing orb smoothly across the canvas, capturing threads within a radius to weave them into connected shapes. The orb’s movement speed and path influence thread attraction and connection dynamics.
concept.scoring_and_end: Points are awarded per completed light pattern formed by connecting threads. The round ends after a 60-second timer, with a visible countdown and score displayed. Replay is encouraged to improve pattern speed and accuracy.
concept.visual_theme: Dark background canvas with vibrant neon-like glowing light threads and a luminous orb. Fluid lighting effects emphasize thread connections and orb interaction, creating a serene, mesmerizing atmosphere.
concept.differentiator: Unlike BoRHeZ’s prior games, this mechanic focuses on smooth continuous one-finger dragging to physically ‘weave’ light threads into patterns rather than tapping, dodging, or paddle control. The tactile feedback and real-time visual weaving are novel, offering a unique sensory mobile experience that is easy to learn but hard to master.

designer.required_evidence: Implementation must demonstrate responsive one-finger drag control reliably capturing and connecting threads, a clear visible timer, scoring increment on completed patterns, pause/resume and restart functionality, stable performance on 360x780 and 390x844 screens with no input lag or UI overflow, and must pass autonomous browser acceptance testing verifying mechanics match this concept without substitutions.

researcher.claim: Propose a fully playable, original HTML5 one-finger mobile minigame concept that is distinct from existing BoRHeZ titles and suitable for implementation within the studio's technical and interaction constraints.
researcher.rationale: The game concept emphasizes a distinctive timing and discovery mechanic where the player controls a single actor on a fixed circular path, tapping to jump inward to collect moving targets and returning to the perimeter to avoid collision with enemies. This core mechanism differs fundamentally from BoRHeZ's existing titles (no survival combat, collect/dodge, paddle-and-break, or ordered embroidery mechanics) and aligns with the required one-finger drag and tap constraint. By limiting control to a single tap timed to jump inward and back to the perimeter, the player learns risk-reward timing and spatial awareness, fostering engagement and mastery. The scoring is based on successful inward jumps to collect targets, with the round ending upon collision or timeout, providing clear goals and replayability. The visual theme of a neon orbit with contrasting moving dots and expanding rings reinforces spatial intuition and emphasizes the timing mechanic's clarity.
researcher.objections: Without playtesting, difficulty tuning (speed of targets/enemies, jump timing) may not perfectly balance challenge and accessibility. The single tap to jump mechanic may require precise timing which could be frustrating on small mobile screens. Reduced-motion support and pointer cancel/re-entry will need considered implementation to ensure smooth gameplay. Ensuring the circular fixed path's responsiveness to one-finger drag might pose minor technical complexity, but drag can be limited to vertical tangent to scroll the path's angle if required. The concept is susceptible to requiring intuitive UI to convey jump timing clearly without confusion.

concept.title: Orbit Jump
concept.core_loop: The player controls an avatar moving at constant speed around a fixed circular orbit around the screen's center, using one-finger drag to slowly adjust orbit speed within limits. Targets periodically appear along the orbit. The player taps once to make the avatar jump inward along the radius to collect a target before quickly returning to the orbit's perimeter. Missing a target or colliding with a moving enemy on the orbit ends the round.
concept.player_action: One-finger drag horizontally to subtly control orbit speed (optional speed adjustments for player agency). One-finger tap initiates a timed jump inward and back out, requiring player to time tap precisely to align with target's position. The avatar automatically returns after jump; player cannot jump again until back on the orbit.
concept.scoring_and_end: Points are scored for each successful inward jump that collects a target. The game ends if the player returns late, misses the target, or collides with an enemy on the orbit path, or after a fixed time limit. Scores and time are displayed in real-time; player can start/pause/restart rounds.
concept.visual_theme: Minimalist neon style with a bright circular orbit ring on dark background. Targets appear as glowing dots moving along the orbit. The avatar is a bright circle that visibly jumps inward with an expanding/trailing ring effect. Enemies are distinct neon colors that move faster to add tension.
concept.differentiator: Combines a novel timing-based jump mechanic from and back to a fixed circular path, blending continuous orbit movement with discrete inward-outward jumps; unlike traditional collect/dodge or paddle games. The player learns to time jumps by spatially anticipating moving targets, creating a simple but engaging timing discovery loop suitable for casual one-finger mobile play.

researcher.required_evidence: Implementation must include: responsive working orbit movement controlled by drag; tap-activated jump animation inward and back; target and enemy movement along orbit; collision detection; scoring display; start/pause/restart buttons; reduced-motion support; stable performance on 360x780 and 390x844 Chromium mobile emulation; fulfill all required game states and diagnostic window.BORHEZ_GAME snapshot exposure; support for pointer cancel and re-entry without game errors. Validation testing confirming core mechanic's playable timing loop and distinctive feel as proposed.

engineer.claim: Propose a one-finger mobile game concept named 'Magnet Maze' featuring a unique polarity switching mechanic combined with maze navigation and timed risk-reward scoring.
engineer.rationale: This concept offers a fresh physical interaction by having the player drag a magnet through a maze while dynamically switching its polarity to attract or repel metallic obstacles. The polarity switching adds a surprising strategic layer beyond typical drag or tap controls, fitting well within a simple one-finger control scheme. The core loop involves balancing safe movement and timed polarity switches to maximize score before time expires, a clear and engaging win/loss condition. The visual theme of a stylized glowing magnetic maze with particle effects is distinct from existing BoRHeZ games. The concept respects the technical constraints including a single canvas area, no external assets, and visible score and state elements.
engineer.objections: Potential difficulty in conveying polarity switching intuitively with one finger could affect accessibility. The game must ensure polarity switching is easily discoverable and responsive to avoid frustration. Another risk is complexity in collision physics within the time constraints of a minigame, so a simplified physics simulation might be necessary. Also, as a novel mechanic, player engagement must be validated through testing to ensure it is immediately fun and not confusing.

concept.title: Magnet Maze
concept.core_loop: The player drags a magnetic orb through a maze. Obstacles in the maze have metallic properties that either attract or repel based on the orb’s polarity. By tapping the orb (still within the one-finger rule), the player switches polarity between positive and negative, toggling attraction and repulsion to navigate around or push away obstacles. The maze and obstacles shift dynamically to increase challenge as time progresses.
concept.player_action: One finger drags the orb to move it and taps the same finger to flip its polarity. Players must tactically time polarity switches to avoid collisions and to reach checkpoints or collect ‘charge’ pickups in the maze.
concept.scoring_and_end: Players score points by reaching checkpoints and collecting charges. Colliding with obstacles ends the game immediately (loss). A timer counts down from 60 seconds; surviving until time expires ends the game (win). The score reflects checkpoint and charge collection, rewarding risk-taking and precision polarity switching.
concept.visual_theme: A neon-lit labyrinth with dark backgrounds. The orb glows distinct colors for polarity states (e.g., blue for negative, red for positive). Metallic obstacles shimmer and react visually with magnetic attraction or repulsion, enhanced by simple particle effects and smooth animations emphasizing polarity changes.
concept.differentiator: Unlike traditional drag or tap games, the polarity switching mechanic requires real-time risk-reward physical interaction with magnetic physics elements, creating an innovative tactile experience within a simple one-finger control scheme. The dynamic maze and timed challenge further differentiate this concept from existing BoRHeZ titles.

engineer.required_evidence: A prototype demonstrating responsive one-finger drag combined with tap-to-switch polarity mechanism, visual feedback for polarity states, simple obstacle interactions showing attraction and repulsion effects, a working timer and score system, and a fail-fast collision detection ending the game on impact. Confirmation via playtests or demo recordings that the polarity switching mechanic is intuitive and engaging within the minigame’s time constraints.

critic.claim: Among the three concept proposals—Lumen Weave (designer), Orbit Jump (researcher), and Magnet Maze (engineer)—Orbit Jump is the preferred candidate due to balanced strengths in originality, first-minute fun, clarity, feasibility, and replay potential, despite some risks requiring targeted mitigations.
critic.rationale: Lumen Weave offers a novel 'weaving' mechanic with continuous touch dragging generating luminous patterns. This is original and visually stunning but may suffer from ambiguous immediate clarity and moderate risk in conveying precise goals and controls at first glance, impacting one-finger clarity and potentially first-minute fun. Magnet Maze combines polarity-switching with drag mechanics in a dynamic maze. Its originality is solid, introducing a physical, tactile nuance to simple dragging; however, complexity in polarity toggling combined with movement dynamics may reduce one-finger clarity and increase player cognitive load, risking accessibility especially on small portrait mobile devices. Both face risks in implementation complexity due to fluid visuals and physics. Orbit Jump presents a novel blend of orbit speed adjustment and timed jump mechanics around a circular path, offering a clear, intuitive one-finger control schema: drag to modulate speed, tap to jump. It involves familiar spatial anticipation but in a fresh context, supporting strong first-minute fun and replay potential through timing mastery. It has a well-bounded scope facilitating feasible implementation and reduced interface ambiguity, making it accessible and suitable as a mobile minigame.

objections.Lumen Weave: Controls and goals might not be immediately apparent, causing confusion or slow onboarding, which could diminish early engagement. Testing if players understand the weaving objective and can control the orb smoothly with one finger is crucial.
objections.Orbit Jump: Speed adjustment via drag may be subtle and require fine-tuning to avoid frustrated users. The jump timing mechanic could be unforgiving if cues are unclear, risking player churn. Testing timing windows, feedback clarity, and responsiveness under mobile constraints is necessary.
objections.Magnet Maze: Two simultaneous control modes (drag + polarity tap) might overload simple one-finger usability; polarity state feedback and interaction complexity may overwhelm casual players. Implementing smooth magnetic physics effects without performance loss can be challenging. Usability and performance tests are critical.

assessments.strength: Strong originality through continuous weaving mechanic; visually captivating neon theme promotes sensory immersion.
assessments.risk: Insufficient immediate clarity of game goals and controls; potential learning curve could hinder first-minute fun.
assessments.mitigation: Add clear tutorial hints, goals display, and simple onboarding to demonstrate orb movement and pattern completion.

assessments.strength: Clear, intuitive one-finger control with distinct drag and tap interactions; novel timing challenge fosters engagement and replayability.
assessments.risk: Subtle speed control drag may confuse or feel unresponsive; jump timing requires good feedback to prevent frustration.
assessments.mitigation: Implement visual and haptic cues for speed changes and jump timing windows; conduct early UI feedback tests on mobile touch devices.

assessments.strength: Innovative polarity switching combined with drag introduces unique tactile physicality; dynamic maze adds challenge progression.
assessments.risk: Complexity of combined controls risks confusing players; magnetic physics may strain mobile performance and impact smoothness.
assessments.mitigation: Simplify polarity toggle responsiveness, enhance visual polarity cues, and profile performance early; test user comprehension and response times.

proposed_action.reason: Orbit Jump achieves a strong balance of originality and one-finger clarity, delivering engaging first-minute gameplay and high replay potential with feasible implementation. Its control scheme is intuitive for mobile users, and risks are manageable with targeted UI and feedback improvements.

required_evidence.Lumen Weave: User comprehension tests of orb control and pattern recognition under one-finger constraints; early engagement timing data to validate first-minute fun; implementation performance profiling for fluid effects.
required_evidence.Orbit Jump: Mobile touch responsiveness tests for drag speed adjustments; player timing accuracy and error rate metrics for jump mechanics; feedback clarity validation (visual, haptic) for interaction cues.
required_evidence.Magnet Maze: Usability assessment of combined drag and tap controls; performance benchmarks on typical mobile devices for magnetic physics; player cognitive load analysis to verify polishing needed controls and tutorial clarity.

producer.claim: The 'researcher' candidate's Orbit Jump concept is the best choice for production.
producer.rationale: Orbit Jump presents a compelling mix of originality and straightforward, one-finger interaction that supports engaging immediate gameplay and replayability. Its mechanic combines continuous orbit movement with timed radial jumps, which is novel and practical for mobile play. The control scheme (simple drag to adjust speed and tap to jump) is intuitive and less likely to confuse players. Critic feedback highlights manageable risks with clear mitigations, making feasibility high. Compared to the complex polarity switching and physics demands of Magnet Maze, or the potentially unclear goals and learning curve of Lumen Weave, Orbit Jump strikes a strong balance that fits project constraints and player expectations.

objections.reason: While highly original and visually immersive, Lumen Weave's complexity and lack of immediate clarity in objectives and controls could hinder player engagement and increase onboarding time, risking drop-off.

Magnet Maze offers an innovative tactile mechanic but faces potential performance issues on mobile devices and risks confusing players due to the dual control scheme and cognitive load from magnetic physics.

proposed_action.selection_reason: Orbit Jump balances fresh, fun gameplay with simple one-finger controls, ensuring immediate player engagement and feasible implementation by addressing manageable UI risks.

rejected_candidates.reason: High originality but risk of unclear goals and steep learning curve that could reduce fun and accessibility on first play.
Innovative mechanic complicated by dual input demands and potential mobile performance issues, risking smoothness and player comprehension.

implementation_directives: Develop clear visual and haptic feedback for orbit speed adjustments and jump timing windows to support intuitive control.
Design minimalistic neon-themed UI elements emphasizing orbit, avatar, targets, and enemies for instant readability.
Implement stable one-finger drag for speed control with responsive delay tuning to avoid unresponsiveness confusion.
Create robust game state management with visible score, timer, pause/resume, and restart functionality.
Test critical path for jump timing accuracy, miss/fail conditions, and smooth avatar movement along orbit and during jumps.

required_evidence: Confirm prototype UI and control responsiveness with mobile touch input tests.
Validate target jump timing and collision detection functionality allow for consistent, frustration-free gameplay.
Ensure no performance degradation occurs during orbit movement and jumping sequences on target devices.
Obtain user feedback on tutorial clarity and immediate game goals comprehension.
Verify game state transitions cover start, pause/resume, restart, end conditions, and score display without errors.

coder_report:
# Orbit Jump implementation

Selected candidate: `researcher` — **Orbit Jump**. Read `job.json`, `plan.json`, and `feedback.md` (empty array). The target directory did not previously exist; there was no existing behavior to preserve.

Implemented only `docs/games/studio-original-003/index.html`, `game.css`, and `game.js`.

## Finished mechanic and criteria

- The mint avatar automatically circles a fixed neon ring. Horizontal one-finger drag adjusts angular speed smoothly within 0.72–1.28 radians/second, visibly moving the actor and updating the speed readout. Left/right arrows and A/D provide equivalent speed control.
- A tap initiates a 0.68-second radial jump inward and automatically returns to the perimeter. Repeated jumps are locked until return. Space, up/down arrows, and W/S also jump.
- Moving gold targets occupy the inner radius of the circular track. A gold launch sector and “JUMP NOW” cue predict the alignment at the inward midpoint. Actual radial proximity and angular overlap collect targets; each awards one point. Visual feedback and optional supported-device vibration mark timing windows, catches, and failure.
- Eight catches win. A failed jump, a target left uncollected for nine seconds, or contact with the faster moving pink enemy on the perimeter loses. The enemy has a five-second opening grace period. A 45-second round deadline also ends the round.
- Score, countdown, speed, ready/running/paused/over state, and outcome are visible. Play starts through a real button event; Pause remains available to resume; Restart resets elapsed time, score, jump, targets, enemy, input, and feedback. Blur/hidden-page events pause gameplay.
- Pointer capture, pointer release/cancellation, and re-entry are handled. Touch gestures are restricted only on the canvas. The responsive portrait layout uses local CSS/JS and no external assets, dependencies, fetches, accounts, or services.
- Reduced-motion preference disables decorative jump rings, catch pulses, glow, and vibration while preserving essential gameplay motion.
- `window.BORHEZ_GAME` is frozen. Each snapshot returns fresh objects containing actual state, elapsed time, score, player position, and additional read-only mechanic details. The HTML build label begins `LOCAL BUILD` and is never changed by game JavaScript.

Concrete tuning choices: targets sit on a concentric inner collection lane so that an inward jump is necessary. Returns are automatic and have a fixed duration rather than a separate manual late-return mechanic. Eight targets provide an explicit early victory within the fixed time limit. These specify the selected orbit/jump loop rather than substituting another concept.

## Checks actually run

- `node --check docs/games/studio-original-003/game.js` — passed, including after implementation.
- `node /tmp/orbit-check.cjs` — passed a VM harness executing the actual unmodified game source with mocked DOM/canvas and controlled animation timestamps. Verified ready/start, elapsed progression, drag speed and actor movement, pointer cancellation, exact paused-time freeze, resume, reset, mistimed-jump loss, accurately timed inward collection with score increment, automatic return, target-expiration loss, and moving-enemy collision loss. This is logic evidence, not browser or rendering QA.
- `node game_factory/mobile_acceptance.cjs` — attempted; could not execute checks because Chromium exited at launch with sandbox socket `Operation not permitted` / SIGTRAP. The gate itself was not modified.
- `curl -I http://127.0.0.1:8765/games/studio-original-003/` — no server was listening. Attempted a temporary local Python HTTP server; socket creation was denied by the environment. No test page was served. Source build label remains untouched.
- `git status --short` — implementation files were the only source additions.
